questions.prompt: The team practices TDD, but the suite takes 25 minutes and people have quietly stopped running it locally. What's the real problem?
options: TDD doesn't scale past a certain codebase size.
Most of those 'unit' tests touch a database or the network. Split them: a genuinely fast suite that runs on every save, and the slow ones in CI.
The CI machines need to be faster.
There are simply too many tests — some should be deleted.
questions.explanation: A test suite you don't run has no value, so speed is a correctness property, not a nicety. Almost always the cause is I/O smuggled into unit tests through a shared Spring context or a test container. The fix isn't fewer tests, it's tests that know which layer they're in.

questions.prompt: This test is green. What's wrong with it?
options: It asserts which methods were called, not what happened. Any refactor breaks it, and it would still pass if the message were addressed to the wrong person.
verify should be replaced with assertThat.
It's missing a @BeforeEach to reset the mocks.
Mockito can't verify three mocks in one test.
questions.explanation: Tests that assert on interactions pin the implementation in place while proving nothing about the outcome — the worst trade available, because they punish exactly the refactoring they were supposed to make safe. Assert on the request that was built or the state that changed. Verifying a call is right when the call itself is the observable effect.

questions.prompt: Limited time to add tests to a service sending billions of messages. Where do they go?
options: Chase line coverage until it's high enough to be a meaningful number.
On the logic that decides who gets which message, and on the idempotency and retry paths — where a bug is both expensive and silent.
End-to-end tests only, since those are the closest thing to reality.
On the controllers, since every request goes through them.
questions.explanation: Test where failure is expensive and invisible. A crash gets noticed in minutes; sending the wrong segment the wrong offer, or delivering a message twice because a retry wasn't idempotent, gets noticed by the customer. Coverage as a target optimises for the easy half of the codebase.

questions.prompt: This test passes but provides weak protection. What is the main red flag?
options: It only proves that some truthy value returned; it does not verify the business outcome, persisted state, emitted event, or important fields.
The function should be mocked even if it is the subject under test.
questions.explanation: A vague truthiness assertion can stay green through serious regressions. A valuable test states the observable contract: which order was created, with what values, and which externally meaningful side effects occurred.
